content.title: Two Sum
content.description: Find two different indices whose values add up to target. Return the indices in either order. Each input has exactly one valid pair.
content.constraints: 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10,000. Values and target are between −1,000,000 and 1,000,000.
content.idea: Ask a smaller question: have I already seen the number that completes this pair? A map turns that question into a lookup.
content.invariant: Before index i, the map contains values from earlier indices only. Check first, then insert, so an element cannot pair with itself.

complexity.tradeoff: A nested loop uses O(1) extra space but takes O(n²) time. The map buys speed with memory.

hints: For each number x, you need target − x.
Store each visited value with its index in a HashMap.
Check the complement before inserting the current number.

frames.message: We need two values that add up to 9. Start with an empty map.
Visit 2. Its complement is 9 − 2 = 7. We have not seen 7 yet.
Remember the value 2 and its index. Check first, then insert.
Visit 7. Its complement is 9 − 7 = 2. Our map has it!
Return indices [0, 1]. The map avoids checking every possible pair.

content.title: Duplicate Detective
content.description: Return true if any integer appears more than once. Return false when every value is unique.
content.idea: A set remembers membership. If adding a value changes nothing, that value was already there.
content.invariant: The set contains every value before the current position.

complexity.tradeoff: Sorting reduces extra storage in some implementations, but costs O(n log n) time and may change the input.

hints: You only need to remember whether a value exists.
HashSet.add returns false for an existing value.

frames.message: A set remembers which values have visited before.
Add 1. This is its first visit.
Add 2. Still unique.
Add 3. No duplicate yet.
The next 1 is already in the set. Return true.

content.title: Anagram Alchemy
content.description: Two lowercase words are anagrams when they use exactly the same letters with the same counts. Decide whether s and t are anagrams.
content.constraints: Only lowercase English letters. 0 ≤ string length ≤ 10,000.
content.idea: Use a 26-slot frequency table. Add for the first word, subtract for the second. Balanced counts mean an anagram.
content.invariant: Each slot tracks the difference between the two prefixes processed so far.

complexity.tradeoff: The fixed alphabet makes 26 counters constant space. General Unicode text needs a different representation.

hints: Start by comparing lengths.
A letter can index a counter using c − 'a'.
Every counter must finish at zero.

frames.message: listen and silent have the same length. Compare letter counts.
frames.note: Count up for s. Count down for t.

frames.message: First count the letters in listen.
Subtract the letters in silent. Each increment is balanced.
Every counter is zero, so return true. Equal lengths alone would not be enough.

content.title: Find the Signal
content.description: Find target in a strictly increasing sorted array. Return its index, or −1 if it does not exist.
content.constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10,000. The array is sorted in increasing order.
content.idea: Sorted order tells you which half cannot contain the target. Discard that half and repeat.
content.invariant: If the target exists, its index is between left and right, inclusive.

complexity.tradeoff: Binary search needs sorted data. Sorting a single unsorted lookup can cost more than a linear scan.

hints: Keep an inclusive interval [left, right].
Use left + (right − left) / 2.
Move past mid after eliminating a half.

frames.message: Search for 9. The whole array is our candidate interval.
The midpoint is index 2, value 3. Since 3 < 9, discard this index and its left side.
The new midpoint is index 4. The value is 9.
Found it! Return 4. Every unsuccessful comparison halves the interval.

content.title: The Insertion Point
content.description: Return the first index whose value is at least target. Return nums.length when every value is smaller. Repeated values are allowed.
content.constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10,000. Values are sorted in nondecreasing order.
content.idea: Search for the boundary between values smaller than target and values at least target.
content.invariant: All indices before left are too small. The answer stays in [left, right].

complexity.tradeoff: The half-open interval makes the end insertion point natural; its update rules differ from exact-match search.

hints: Start right at nums.length.
Keep a possible answer by setting right = mid.
Stop when the boundaries meet.

frames.message: Find the first value at least 3. Use [left, right) with right = 4.
Value 3 qualifies, but there may be an earlier one. Keep mid as a candidate.
Value 3 qualifies again. Move right to 1.
Value 1 is too small. Everything through index 0 can be discarded.
left equals right. Index 1 is the first qualifying position.

content.title: Square & Compare
content.description: Square every value in a sorted array and return the squares in nondecreasing order. Try a linear-time solution.
content.idea: The largest remaining square is at one end. Fill the answer from right to left.
content.invariant: Everything after write index i is already in its final sorted position.

complexity.tradeoff: The returned array takes O(n) space. Squaring and sorting is simpler but costs O(n log n).

hints: A large negative number can have a large square.
Compare absolute values at both ends.
Write the largest square at the back.

frames.message: Compare absolute values at both ends. The larger square goes at the back.
|10| beats |−4|. Place 100 at the end and move right inward.
|−4| beats |3|. Place 16 next and move left inward.
|3| beats |−1|. Place 9.
Place 1, then 0. Filling from the back keeps the result sorted.

content.title: Mirror Words
content.description: Ignore ASCII punctuation and spaces, and compare letters without case. Return whether the remaining text reads the same forward and backward.
content.constraints: 0 ≤ s.length ≤ 10,000. Input contains ASCII characters only. An empty normalized string is a palindrome.
content.idea: Two readers start at opposite ends, skip punctuation, and compare one meaningful character at a time.
content.invariant: All meaningful characters outside the two pointers have already matched.

complexity.tradeoff: Building a cleaned string is easier to inspect but uses O(n) extra memory.

hints: Use one pointer at each end.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters before comparing.
Compare lowercase characters.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
tests.label: Ignore punctuation

frames.message: Compare the outer characters of abba.
a equals a. Move both pointers inward.
b equals b. This pair matches too.
The pointers crossed. Every pair matched: return true.
frames.note: When reading real input, skip punctuation first.

content.title: Zero Gravity
content.description: Move all zeroes to the end while preserving the order of nonzero values. Modify nums and return the same array.
content.constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10,000. Preserve the relative order of nonzero elements.
content.idea: Use a read pointer to explore and a write pointer to build a compact nonzero prefix.
content.invariant: Before write, the array contains the nonzero values encountered so far, in their original order.

complexity.tradeoff: Writing twice is straightforward. Swapping can avoid some writes but needs careful handling.

hints: Track the next position for a nonzero value.
Copy nonzero values first.
Fill the remaining suffix with zeroes.

frames.message: Read each value. write marks the next slot for a nonzero value.
Read 1 and copy it to index 0. Advance write.
Read 0. Skip it; leave write where it is.
Read 3 and copy it to index 1.
Read 12 and copy it to index 2. The useful prefix is complete.
Fill the remaining positions with zeroes. The nonzero order is unchanged.

content.title: One Good Trade
content.description: You may buy once and sell on a later day. Return the greatest possible profit, or zero when no profitable trade exists.
content.idea: Carry the cheapest price seen so far. Each day asks: what if I sell today?
content.invariant: lowest is the minimum price up to this day; best is the best profit from all processed days.

complexity.tradeoff: Checking every pair of days takes O(n²). A running minimum removes that repeated work.

hints: The purchase must happen before the sale.
Remember the smallest price in the prefix.
Compare today's profit with the best so far.

frames.message: Start with the first price. You cannot make a profit yet.
1 is a new lower purchase price. Remember it.
Selling at 5 after buying at 1 earns 4.
Selling at 3 would earn 2. Keep the better profit.
Selling at 6 improves the profit to 5.
4 gives a smaller profit. Return the best seen, 5.

content.title: Window Shopping
content.description: Find the largest sum of any contiguous group of exactly k values. Return the sum.
content.idea: A fixed-size window changes by just two values: one leaves and one enters. Reuse the previous sum.
content.invariant: sum is always the sum of the current window of exactly k values.

complexity.tradeoff: Recomputing every window takes O(nk). Incremental updates take constant work per move.

hints: Compute the first k-value sum.
Subtract the value leaving the window.
Add the entering value and update the maximum.

frames.message: The first width-4 window sums to 2.
Slide once: subtract 1 and add 50. No need to rescan the middle.
Slide again: subtract 12 and add 3. The new sum is 42.
Return the largest sum seen: 51.

content.title: Bracket Buddies
content.description: Check whether every opening bracket has the correct closing bracket in the correct nesting order.
content.idea: The most recent opening bracket must close first. A stack stores the closing brackets you expect next.
content.invariant: From top to bottom, the stack contains the required closing brackets in order.

complexity.tradeoff: A counter works for one bracket type but cannot enforce nesting across different types.

hints: Nesting follows last-in, first-out order.
Push the closing bracket you expect.
The stack must be empty at the end.

frames.message: A stack remembers the closing brackets we expect.
Read {. Push its partner }.
Read [. Its partner ] must close before }.
Read ]. It matches the stack top, so pop it.
Read }. It matches and empties the stack. Return true.

content.title: The Fibonacci Forest
content.description: Return Fibonacci number n, where F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, and F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2).
content.constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 40. The result fits in a Java int.
content.idea: The next number only needs the last two. Keep those two states instead of recomputing a recursion tree.
content.invariant: At iteration i, a = F(i) and b = F(i+1).

complexity.tradeoff: Naive recursion repeats work exponentially. Memoization helps but uses O(n) space.

hints: Write down the two base values.
Carry only the previous two numbers.
Move both states forward at the same time.

frames.message: Start with the base cases. These anchor every later result.
Start with the base cases. These anchor every later result.
Add the previous two states: 0 + 1 = 1. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 1 + 1 = 2. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 1 + 2 = 3. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 2 + 3 = 5. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 3 + 5 = 8. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.

content.title: Common Ground
content.description: Find the greatest common divisor of two nonnegative integers. For this exercise, gcd(0, 0) is defined as 0.
content.idea: Euclid's key observation: replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b) preserves their common divisors.
content.invariant: The greatest common divisor stays unchanged after every remainder step.

complexity.tradeoff: Testing all possible divisors is intuitive but much slower for large numbers.

hints: Repeat until the remainder is zero.
The last nonzero divisor is the answer.

frames.message: Euclid's algorithm keeps the GCD unchanged while shrinking the problem.
48 % 18 = 12. Replace the pair with (18, 12).
18 % 12 = 6. Replace the pair with (12, 6).
12 % 6 = 0. Stop: the answer is 6.

content.title: Prime Time
content.description: Count the prime numbers strictly smaller than n. A prime is greater than 1 and has exactly two positive divisors.
content.idea: The sieve marks multiples instead of testing every number separately. Start at p² because smaller multiples were already covered.
content.invariant: After processing p, every composite with a prime factor at most p has been marked.

complexity.tradeoff: Trial division uses less storage but repeats divisibility checks.

hints: Use an array to mark composite numbers.
For each unmarked p, mark multiples starting at p².
Count unmarked indices from 2 to n−1.

frames.message: Count primes strictly below 10. Start with candidates from 2 onward.
2 is prime. Mark its multiples starting at 2² = 4.
3 is prime. Mark its multiples starting at 3² = 9.
The unmarked numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7. Return 4.

content.title: Stairway to Java
content.description: Reach step n by taking one or two steps at a time. Return the number of different step sequences. There is one way to stay on step zero.
content.idea: Your final move comes from step n−1 or n−2. Add the number of ways to reach those two smaller states.
content.invariant: previous and current hold the counts for the two most recent steps.

complexity.tradeoff: A full DP table makes intermediate states easy to inspect, but only two states are needed.

hints: Think about the final move.
ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2).
Start from ways(0) = ways(1) = 1.

frames.message: Start with the base cases. These anchor every later result.
Start with the base cases. These anchor every later result.
Add the previous two states: 1 + 1 = 2. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 1 + 2 = 3. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 2 + 3 = 5. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.
Add the previous two states: 3 + 5 = 8. Keep only those two numbers for the next step.

content.title: The Best Stretch
content.description: Find the greatest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray. The answer can be negative.
content.idea: At each value, choose between extending the previous stretch and starting a fresh one. This is Kadane's algorithm.
content.invariant: endingHere is the best nonempty subarray ending at this index; best is the largest seen anywhere.

complexity.tradeoff: Enumerating all ranges repeats sums. Tracking the best ending here compresses the useful state.

hints: A negative prefix can hurt the next stretch.
Compare nums[i] with endingHere + nums[i].
Initialize from nums[0], so negative-only inputs work.

frames.message: Initialize from the first value. A nonempty answer may be negative.
Start fresh at 1: it is better than extending the sum −2.
Extend to −2. The overall best stays 1.
Start fresh at 4. A negative prefix would reduce the sum.
Extend through −1, 2 and 1. The running sum reaches 6.
The remaining values never improve on 6. Return 6.
